segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This conversation with George Torgerson took place at his home in Clarkston on May 17, 1976. The Sam Schrager was Sam Schrager.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: In early days, when I was a youngster, why then, about 4:30 in the morning was when we'd get up, see. And then we'd have our chores to do. And then, about 6:30 then, something like that, why then, they'd holler breakfast was ready. And, of course, the time that we'd done chores and this and that, you know, we'd already worked up pretty good appetite. And so breakfast was a pretty big meal. And, you know, that still stays with me. I've got to have breakfast. And, for some reason or another, no sir, that's really my best meal is breakfast.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What would the chores be you'd do from 4:30 to 6:30?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, gosh, we'd have to take care of the horses and milk the cows and take care of the pigs, look after the chickens and all that stuff. Yeah, there right now, we kept real busy in the mornings. So, and then, of course, as soon as breakfast was over with, well then it was to get out in the field or whatever work we had to do. That is the day as it come around then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you need light? When you get up at 4:30, it would still be dark, wouldn't it?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, no, it would just be getting good daylight. Yeah, it would just be getting daylight, not such a good thing to get around. Now, we had 14 head of horses and then we had, well, we dunked when I was just a kid, 8 or 9 cows. And so we kept our mischief. Yeah, we kept our mischief.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Had your parents been there for long before you were born?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I tell you, I'm not right, sure, but I think it was in 1984 or 1985 that they came there. And, of course, I was born in 1992.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they pick where they wanted to homestead, in the valley?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes. Yes, there was only about four, three or four other in the valley there. Swenson's wasn't there at that time. But they come right shortly afterwards.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your father ever, did you ever get an idea about what made him pick, where he picked to homestead?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, as he grew up as a boy, he grew up in the timber and worked in the woods, see. And that was his ambition, he just liked the timber. And now the first year when they come out from Minnesota, well, then they lived up there to Genesee. And while he was there at Genesee, he looked around, so then he got adrift in there and there's where he settled.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Had he come from Norway?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes. Yeah, he was nine years old when he came along. My mother, she was fourteen. So, they both come across the pond… yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, I'd like to talk to you a little bit about what life was like there in Park. Was it a close community, would you say?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, yes, it was that. It was a nice place to live, a real, real nice place to live. So, they, and of course, then, oh, that must have been in 1914, I guess, 15. Then, of course, a lot of them, well, as they began, homesteaders got in there, see, and then they, they taken up, well, they taken up more of that timberland and that, then that, and most of it was more valuable for timber than anything else. So, and it was sold, that is, they sold with a potlatch. There's where the potlatch, PFI, they bought up a lot of that timber for just a little amount. People sold their timber, but not their land. Oh, yeah, them homesteaders that homesteaded like that, well, then they sold everything. Oh, I see. Yeah, land and all.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, did that cause much of a decline in the, in the number of people in the area?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, you bet it did. And now, I don't know just how many there is that lives in Park there now, but there isn't too many. Because, of course, now, I, I imagine, I think Bowman's still owns, that is, our old home place there. And, and then, of course, Sam Anderson, then, he was quite a holder, that is. Now, my, he had my uncle, he homesteaded down, well, right at the porch of where the, where potlatch and Boulder Creek comes in. And he was just upon the point there. And Sam Anderson, he bought that, and he bought up quite a little along the edge there, too. So, between Sam Anderson and Powell and Bowman, well, then, they, they practically had all of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How much did your family have?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: We had, well, my dad, he had 240 acres, and then my brother and I, we bought 40 acres each off in the school section. So, that was what we had. It seemed to me that the, that Park was kind of isolated where it was. I mean, not, it wasn't very easy from, to get from there to a lot of places. No, I tell you, our roads were, they were hard and they were rough to get over. I, well, most of my folks are married there at the cemetery, so I go over there every decoration day, well, then I try to get over. And I can't help but think how nice it is, that is, to drive in there now in a car, and what it used to be. And a lot of people, they, even the road of today, well, then they gripe about it, see, that, that, well, it's chug-holds like that. My gosh, I know that, well, about the time I left there, well, then I didn't, well, I had a car, but I never used it only in the summertime, because in the wintertime, well, then you just couldn't, couldn't use it. And, gosh, you know, in the spring of the year, I think, well, now, about the time that I can begin to use, my, my, well, it was at, oh, Commercial Dodge, what they called it at that time. And, golly, with, you know, I start down the road and get into ruts and high center and dig around and try to get something under the wheels. So, and, so I think, the way I look at it now, well, then, we haven't got, they haven't got much gripe a-comin', because they always, always can get through without too much grief.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, didn't they actually have to do some road building themselves, the people apart?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: In your early days?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, they did. You bet. Yes, they, they had to build. And the first road that they built out of there, well, then, let me see, there was seventeen switchbacks in all on both sides. And there was ten on one and seven on the other.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did this road go?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, it come out on the Upper Anna, Texas Ridge. That's where the old road come out, was at the Upper Anna, Texas Ridge.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And the men of Park built that by hand, pretty much?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, pick and shovel. You bet, in them days, it was all pick and shovel. They must have done that besides all the other work that they had to do, too. Oh, sure. Yes, you bet. No, that's one thing I think that that's why, you know, the lifespan at that time was much shorter than what it is now. And I think it's just all that heavy work that they done.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did both your parents do a lot of heavy work?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, they, they, they, they done a lot of work. My mother, she used to make cheese. And my dad, he'd take it to Kendrick, sometime here to Lewiston. And, and they, they really had to work, you know, that's...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you say she was busy from morning till night, from when she got up to when she went to sleep, your mother?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: That's right. Yeah, she'd have something to do. She, well, it was, my dad, he'd been married before, and he had two children. And so then, and then there was eight of us. So that made ten. And, you know, you take ten hungry kids, it keeps them pretty busy.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where, where did the family's food come from? And was it mostly stuff that you grew and parked when, when you were a kid growing up?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yeah. That is one thing that, you might say the only thing that we bought from town was flour, sugar, and coffee, and the like of that. We, and the rest of it, by then we grew. We, we could go to the store at that time and buy like we do now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How often would you be likely to go into town?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, my dad, I'd, every, oh, two or three weeks or something like that, you know. And then we, the mother, she'd have butter and eggs and like that to send in, and that took care of most, most of the groceries. So, and as far as, one didn't see too many dollars. So, but anyhow, I don't know, I was just thinking here the other day. At that time, why, we, of course it was horse and wagon days, but if we met a neighbor, we always had time to talk half an hour, an hour, or something like that. And of course, today, why then, we haven't got time for, to talk to anybody practically. So, but...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What's the difference, I wonder?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, it's, now, why then everything seems to be more in, well, hurry up. Just hurry along. We, and, gosh, you know, we, so that's, that must be it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you and the neighbor would, would talk, what, what, I'm just wondering, what would be the kinds of things that, that friends would talk about in a community like Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, it would be, that is, how he was getting along, and what he thought of the crops that year, and so on, and, and then of course they'd also ask about some of the other neighbors, how they were getting along, if he'd seen them lately, and like that. So, they'd always pick up a pretty good conversation.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you say getting along, makes me think, did, did most of the people there at Park, were most of them able to get along well enough that they would stay in those early years, or did many people leave because it was so hard?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Very few that left there. There was very few. And that is at the early stage, when it was very few that left there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It just seems to me awful hard to imagine, now I guess that's because I'm young and it's a whole different time, but to imagine, I've heard a lot of people talk about it, that pioneering life sounds really rough to me for families to, to, to get through. And I wonder how the people in Park pulled through that kind of thing, and how many, most of the people could stay, and not give up in despair.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, it seemed as though that they just stayed, and of course, they, they all, as far as that, they had plenty to eat, and of course, they, by working, and of course now, at harvest time, at one time, there was no harvesting done in there. And then, people would go out and harvest, and then they'd make a little extra money there, and now my dad, he had a thrashing machine, and he used to thrash on American Ridge and around there, and of course he made a little extra money there, too, and so, and...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would his crew be men from Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, some of them would, and then others, he'd pick up them wherever they might be, that is where he was thrashing, see. Well, it sounds like he did fairly well then, perhaps. Oh, yeah, we, we got along fairly good. Although, you take the rest of them that was there, you know, they got by also. Of course, the one thing they had to do was, they eat, well then, we had to garden. And, and that, which is quite an item, that is, you know, especially for a large family, by the way.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about learning to talk English?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, when I started in, I was just about half. I was just about half Norwegian and half English. And then, of course, as time went on, well then, well then, of course, it changed over a little bit. Although, I better say, my English is not too good yet. Well, your English sounds fine to me. So, hey, yeah. No, it sounds fine to me. I'm just thinking about, I'm thinking well in a community where most of the people were Norwegian, as I think Park was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You wouldn't have too much incentive to start talking English, would you? I mean, you'd, kids would all be born.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, of course, us kids and like that, well then, of course, that's what we'd done. Ed and I, we'd always talk Norwegian. And, but then, of course, as time went on, then, when we began to go to school, well then, we'd have to change over, because that's what they had. They had the teachers, the English, so we had to change over.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was school like for you?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, I enjoyed it. Yes, I enjoyed the school. Because, although at that time, well then, we'd have three months in the fall and four months in the summer. That's what we had.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Four months in the summer?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, it was four months the other way. I'm vice versa. Three months in the summer and four months in the winter. In the winter, yeah. Of course, it'd be towards fall, that is when school would commence… so, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the community church there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, now, it was built, now I forget just when that was built. And, of course, Lewiston, that's what they were, seeing all the people around there in Lewiston. Now, I was baptized, Lewiston was also confirmed. And, so, and it was too bad. Now, that was a nice little church. And, we used to gather there, that is on decoration day, all us younger people then. And, the roof began to leak. And, so then, we mentioned about the roof, that we should put a new, well, put a tin roof on it. And, so then, there was some folks there by the name of DeGroff. They bought in there of later years. And, the boy, he worked there at Troy for the Troy Aluminum Company. So, that it was left to him to see what they could be bought for, that is the tin and whatnot. But, some way or another, well then, he went away, that is he went east, something come up. And, it was never anything done. And, you know, that's what ruined that little church. If we'd have gotten the roof on it, so it had a leak, as far as the foundation and that, well then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long ago was that, that you were going to put a roof on it?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, gosh, you know, I don't just remember.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When people got together for decoration day, was that when you still lived there, in Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, I lived in Moscow at that time. Yeah. No, I left Park, it was in 1925, when I left Park.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that church used a lot when you lived in Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, it was used quite a little bit, yeah. The minister, he used to live out, well there was no fellow by the name of Anderson, and he lived out by dairy, and he used to come in.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Every Sunday?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, but, oh, sometimes every two weeks, and maybe it would go as much as a month. But, then, the other doings, well then, they'd have a little something going on, by themselves, and that would be in the church, and of course then the Schuylkill House was there also. Yeah, Ed and I, we went to school in the old log school house. When you say doings, tell me a little bit about what kind of doings they were. Oh, it might be social gatherings, or something like that, see. And then, of course, Christmas, we'd always have to have a Christmas tree and celebrate Christmas.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: At the school, or in the church?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, they were both down at the school.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: On your home?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Burnt, it burnt everything that we had.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How did that happen?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, at that time it was stovepipes. See, just a tin pipe, and we thought that that's what started it, was that it gathered a bunch of stuff around it, and of course, you take one of them old houses, you know, and the stuff inside of it, by then, it burnt, and burnt fast. So, that lost quite a lot of the things there, and then, folks then, they bought a place in Juliaetta after they left park, they bought a place in Juliaetta, and that burnt. And so, and among that, by then, practically all the pictures was burnt up, that is them that was back. I'm going to look for this. There was a fellow by the name of… emory Oakeson, he was, well, he was postmaster and that there, and so then he says to me, he says, you know, he says, this is going to be sold, and he says it's going to be sold cheap. And so then, anyhow, then I made a deal for it, and I kept it, oh, I don't know, I guess I had it four or five years. And then, I doubled my money on it, and so I, anyhow, everywhere I've been, if I doubled my money, well, then I'd always sell. So, that's what I done there in Diggory too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This fire, when your parents' home burned down, it must have been a terrible experience for the kids and the parents.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, I'll tell you right, now, it was, it was, it was real rough, and it was the second day of January, when this happened, right in the wintertime, you know. But, oh, I don't know, I think it was along April, that then we had a house so we could move into it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you do from January to April?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, now, we, we had a little store building there. At one time, well, then, we had the park post office. And, so we used it some, and I stayed up there with Ed Swenson's folks a lot of the time, and so we, we fared fairly good. To me, the neighbors were good to us, so we fared pretty good. And, of course, after we got built up, then, someone would get a little of this, a little of that, so we, we fared all right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your father build that new house himself there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, with the help of the neighbors and that, why, then.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So the neighbors pitched in to help you build it?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yes. Yeah. That was common, then, to have, I mean, you could count on the help of the neighbors if you needed help. Right. Right. That was, that was really the nice part of, of that community and, and the way the people done at that time, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: This store, you actually had a store in Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Your parents did?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Post office in the little store. Oh, it was small. Gosh, let me see, I think it was about 16 by 20, 22. That was the size of the building. So, you know, it was pretty, pretty small for it to be a store and post office. But anyhow, I then, my sister, Sheila, taken care of it, and it, he brought in a little money, too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How long did you have the post office and store there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, gosh, no. I just don't remember. But it was in the early 19, well, we had the post office when it burned. So I'd say that it was right at the 1900s when we, when the post office went in.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your father keep stock in the store pretty regular?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yeah, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did, what was most of the stuff that you, stock that you would sell to people?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, it would be sugar, coffee, and likes of that, you know. That was what we sold. Well, we had bacon and also cheese and like that, so it was, and it hit, well, I don't know just what the gross would be, but it wasn't too, too bad.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you sell any dry goods? Like, bows?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No. We didn't do...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is this your place here?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And is that the school there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: That's the school.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you were right next to the school.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, the school. Here's the church.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I see Potlach Lumber Company already owned quite a bit of that land. That's land that people had sold to them already?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: They'd already sold to them already.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where was your home place, your parents' place?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, here's where we lived. This was my home place right here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about your parents? Is that their place?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, my parents', see. Oh, nice language. Well, there's where I was born. Oh, I see. Yeah, there's where I was born. So you were right next to Ed Swenson. Yeah, just a quarter of a mile across… yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Are there any events that happened in Park or, you know, particular things that happened that struck you as being a little different from what, you know, standing out?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, I don't know if there is or was. Because there wasn't too much, you know. All of them, they behaved themselves pretty good so that they wasn't in any trouble of any kind. So there wasn't anything we might say. And, of course, we'd meet. They'd have a dance at the home, wherever that might be. Well, then they'd pile the chairs up in the corner somewhere. Some did that. But then I think most of it, though, was well from outsiders.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I'm thinking about looking at that and seeing how much land that Potlatch Lumber Company owned. Did that bring much money into the community when they came in?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, it didn't. Because you might say that down there, like them fellows that had homesteaded and that for the... and that was timberland. A lot of that was white pine and like that. And, of course, that's what they were looking for. So, whenever they sold one, then, of course, then they left. And that's why they... Oh, I don't know what the population was at that point in time. Gee, there was quite a few of us there. And, like I say of today, now I don't know. There isn't too many there. And that's what has happened to it. They just...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could you grow? Could you make much money on the farming in there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, at that time, of course, now, my dad... we had ten acres a week. My dad says to me, he says, now I'm going to give you that. All right? And I forget how many bushels it was. It was about thirty some odd bushels in an acre. Now, why did you think I got for that to haul it into Deary? Why did you think I got a bushel for that? Forty-five cents a bushel. That's what I sold my wheat for. And now I'm thinking about, of today, well, then, it's a dollar and sixty something, I think is what the market is today. So, you know, that wasn't too much per acre. But anyhow, we accepted whatever we got and, of course, spent accordingly.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did many people work for Potlatch when they came in and started logging in there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, there wasn't too many, although there was quite a few that worked there with them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I know Charlie Jellibert did.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, Charlie, he worked there with them. Well, when they logged off the section, the school section there, well then, I still lived there on the old home place, see. And, anyhow, I worked out there, I skidded logs out there on the school section. Well, I worked for them over in, when they worked out for River Tooten. Boom, I worked out in the woods.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is that what you did mostly when you grew up? Worked in the woods?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Quite a little bit, yeah. After I grew up and got so that I was kind of supposed to do a little for myself, that's when I got my work done.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have to live in the lumber camps away from home?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yeah. Yeah, yeah. And at that time, well then, you had to carry your own blankets with you. They didn't furnish any blankets. All they had was a bunk. They had double bunks. And, they had mattresses filled with straw. And that's what we put our blankets down on. That's the way we slept. Yeah, you bet you yes. Poor Charlie, if he was here today, he could tell you. I talked to him when he lived in Park. When he was still in Park, yeah. Yeah, I'm pretty sure that that was in Charlie's time too. Now, I was older than Charlie. And, but I'm pretty sure that he was carrying his. I heard, I've heard that those conditions were pretty bad in the camps. Tell the world they built a log cabin, see. And, well now, there at Tobolvo, I think that one that I slept in was about 80 feet long. And, they had two big stoves in there. And I forget how many of us that was in there. But there was better than 50 or 60, about 50 or 60 of us. And, you know, come in and wet and like that, hang up your stuff around the stove and that. You can imagine how, what that was like. In a place like that, you know. And, I never liked the idea of this striking stuff. I never, and I thought when the IW's, when they struck, well years and years ago, you remember, you've read of it. I don't suppose he was here at that time, but then, well I thought, you know, well now, that isn't right. That isn't right. But, I bet today, if they hadn't have struck, we would have still been carrying our, bedding on our backs and sleeping on an old mattress. And that. Because, but, they finally, they had to come to it. And it was the strike that made them. That was the strike that made them. So, of course, I think, really think, that when Nixon, when he froze, oh that was, well, several years ago, you know, he froze a bunch of the stuff at that time. And, then three months, about three months, well then, everything was open again. And you know, of course, there is a man of their degrees with me. But you know, I think, if he'd have froze everything at that time, no strikes, no nothing, everything stayed right at that level, I really believe. And then, when he did, well, let the trade and competition work it out. And, at that time, well then, you know, of today, it's too high. You know, the money now, our dollar isn't worth much. So, and I think that, and still, now they're striking, and sure, they got to give them their allowances, whatever they want. But, I wish somebody could tell me what, how this is going to level off. I don't know, I can't answer that. I wish I knew more.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Listen, when you worked there, for Potlatch, and they, was the pay that you got, the money that you got for the work, enough for you to really get ahead very much?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No. Well, one didn't. You didn't get ahead much. So, about anyhow, I done, it was a little extra money, but as far as getting ahead much, well then, we didn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But you really couldn't make a living on the land that you had at Park, wasn't it? You couldn't make a living just on that?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, now, as far as my folks, well then, I didn't live there too long after I was married, see. I didn't live there too long. But, as far as my folks, well then, my dad, they made a living there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Farming, briefly?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Farming, cattle, some hogs, and all of that. But, anyhow, well then, my dad, well then, he never worked out, I just used to say, worked out in the woods or anything like that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, why did you decide to leave Park and not to stay there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I, with me, well then, I just kinda just, I was just, from year to year, I was just about on the same level. And so, I thought, well, and then I had a brother, and he went to Elk River, and he, so, well, the two brothers, and they went up there, and then they bought into the, well, it was a drain line, and worked like that around the city. And so then, I just kinda made up my mind that I was going to quit farming, and so that's why I went to Elk River.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You had been farming then?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh yes, yes, I had been farming. No,… i never owned this place, that is, that was my folks' place. So, but. I thought you said you did get 40. Yeah, I had 40 acres in here, but as far as the home place there, I didn't. And then, my dad did, seven miles from there, and that was towards Elk River, well then, he had a meadow, and we run cattle there too, so.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you spend much time in the woods between Park and Elk River then?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, whenever I had a little spare time, well then I'd go to the woods. If I had a little spare time, well, I'd go out in the woods, but still, I helped the folks around home there. Well, they really had more than they could take care of.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you run the cattle?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, we had, oh, 100 heads, about, a little better than that. So, oh yes, I used to, I got so, I thought that I was a real cowboy and a rider and all that, till I, I, I, I, a little bit of a horse. Well, it would just hardly, you could hardly just get the saddle on it, and it throwed me so high and so far, and when I got through with that ride, never again… yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, going to, had you been to Elk River before the town started there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember when Turnbull was there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was it at that time when Turnbull was there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, they had the post office, and they had a little store, and of course, that was their livelihood, and then of course they raised cattle, and as far as, oh, they raised some vegetables, not because it was pretty frosty. But, oh, now like carrots and beets and cabbage and like that, you know, I never has raised as nice a carrots and parsnips and cabbage and like that, that entry as is Elk River. Believe me now, and if the frost didn't get the potatoes, another one could raise nice potatoes there, but you know, it was very seldom that, there wasn't a month, and some month, well then they'd have a frost.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was, did Turnbull have a family? Was he the only one at Elk River? Was he the only person, the only family there? Were there others?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, they were the ones, they were their home. Yeah, when they sold out to the Potlatch, well then, they were the ones. Yeah, there was, let me see, you know, there was Willard and his wife, and then they had a boy, and they, Seal. I always thought that was so funny. They had a boy named Seal.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Seal?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Seal, and they were the ones that had, and he'd bought up, well, his dad, but he wasn't there but a short time until he passed away. And, but anyhow, well then, they had a little extra money, and they bought up a lot of that timberland around there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who, the Turnbulls did?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, they bought from them homesteaders, see, and then of course they had all this here, when they sold to the Potlatch then, what, they, I don't know how many hundred acres that they sold to the Potlatch. They had been homesteaders around Elk River, right in the area that the Turnbulls bought their land. Yeah, that's right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wonder were they even had enough money to buy the land?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh yeah, the Turnbulls, they had money. They were moneyed people, and now, there are this Willard's dad, well then, he, without any doubt, well then he had, but at that time, of course, it didn't take too much money, because if they got a thousand or fifteen hundred or something like that, well they thought that they were getting a good price. So it didn't take too much money at that time, but still, they bought up a lot of it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is that what a homestead would go for at that time, maybe a thousand dollars?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, a thousand, or, I don't think they, well it never went over two thousand.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Like when Potlatch bought up the land around Park, was it the same, a thousand dollars or fifteen hundred for a hundred sixty acres?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Pretty much so, yeah, pretty much so. Well, around Turnbulls, then, there were homesteaders around there as well. Yeah, they went in and homesteaded. There was, oh gosh, I know when my folks lived there, well then, it was just kind of a stopping place between Kendrick there and Elk River.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And, at Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: At Park. And so then, gee, there wasn't a night but what, there was somebody staying there, and they were headed for that part of the country to take up homestead. And, of course, the homestead, and then they called it the Stolen Timber also. That was the Stolen Timber Act. And, so, they, and that was, oh, oh I suppose nineteen, yes, it was before the ten, because Potlatch, they went in there in nineteen-nine.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would people stay with you parents on their way through, or where would they stay at Park?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, they'd stop and eat, and they were with my parents, and we always had someplace for them to sleep, but they was caught during the night, like there was, we'd always fix someplace, because we had a pretty good sized house. And they were going to homestead. And that's what they were doing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think they were taking up homesteads there with in mind the idea of selling out to Potlatch later?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, now them fellows that was taken up right at the early days there, they planned to sell to Turnbull. That's what they planned to do. Yeah, they planned to sell to Turnbull. Hmm. But Turnbull never thought, I wonder if he ever thought of developing the area. I mean, all he was doing was, he had a, he was running some stock, and he had a kind of a lodge, didn't he, for people to hunt at, fish at. Yeah, fish and like that, that's right. So, but anyhow, well then, Turnbull, he had a nice sum of money there when he sold to them, because all them homesteaders, well then they sold, I don't know if there was any that sold to the, right out to the Potlatch.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever talk to Turnbull?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of a guy was he?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I think he was a pretty nice fellow, of course, it was like they all said that, it's them that went there and fished and like that. They said, well, that's one thing, he looks out for himself. But as far as that goes, well then he was pretty nice.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, there was never a community around there like there was a park, was there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No. No, there never was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I'm wondering how many people ever did homestead around Elk River. I know we couldn't figure it out exactly, but I'm wondering how many homesteaders were in that area.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I wouldn't know how many either, but there was a good many. Well, there was a good many of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you remember when Potlatch put the mill in Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yeah. My dad and I, at that time we'd sold the cattle and then the hay that we raised off from that meadow, well then we hauled it and sold it, that is, at Elk River when they first started up there. So. Now there's a picture of Elk River, the mill, or part of it there, it isn't all of it. And I think that was taken on about 1914 or maybe 12 or 14. I ain't sure of that either. And it just gets part of it, it isn't the whole... Let me see, you mentioned something about Les Clark last evening. Yeah, I was talking to Mrs. Clark on the phone. Now Les, of course, he took that to Elk River, that picture, but he had gotten, well...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It became a boom town overnight, didn't it?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yes, pretty much so. That really put a lot of people to work. If you shut that off, I got a little story I'm going to tell you about Nigger Joe.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, can't we put it on tape? I like the... We've been trying to get all the stories we can about him. We really want the stories about him.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, this old Nigger Joe, he lived at that time named Janesville. You know, there was a saloon and... Oh, that's years and years ago, too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Lawrence's place.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Lawrence's, yeah, right, Russell Lawrence. So, anyhow, when the PFI, when they came to start the WI and M from Palouse, see, and into Bovill. By then, one of the fellow says that, or one of the head fellow says, he met somebody and he says, Do you know of anybody that drives, or has four horses and would haul freight for us? And so this fellow says to him, he says that, yes, he says there's a colored man that lives up by what they call Janesville. And he says he's a good horseman and got good horses, but of course says he's a colored man. And fellow says, I don't give a darn what color he is. If he's got good horses and will haul freight, why, he says, you bet. Well, he says, I'll send him down here, he says, to you so you can meet up with him. And so he did. So, old nigger Joe, he says that the first evening that he was there, he says that, of course, says, I held my place. He says, I got in the back and sat there, and he says, I know where these fellow, they keep a-looking at me and looking at me. I thought to myself, well, that's just all right. We'll get acquainted. Some of these times, he says, but next evening, he says, the curiosity then, he says, they had to come over and begin a visit. And so he says that, it isn't often that a colored man is out in this kind of weather, because it was cold and snowing and that. Oh, he says, you know, he says that, I'm toughing into it. He says, I've been in this part of the country quite a while, so he says, I'm tough, he says. And he says to them, now, up there where you live, is there a colony of you folks?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: And he says, no, sir, no, sir. He says, it's just me and my wife and three children, all the rest of them up there are Swedes, and we're the only white people about them. I'll never forget that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you think that that would happen when outsiders would come in that wouldn't know the Wells family, that they would just naturally assume that somehow, that, you know, being as he was black, that he wasn't a part of the community like the other people?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, I'll tell you, he got to be just, when we'd meet up with old Joe, well, he used to bale hay for us on that round meadow. And, you know, he, with us folks around there and that, we didn't think anything more of that black than anything at all. Well, I was thinking about outsiders, people that come into the country like Potlatch, you know. Well, of course, now, them fellows from the Potlatch, well, then, of course, they come from Wisconsin, Michigan, the like of that. And, of course, they didn't never think about that, but it wasn't long until they would just go with him just the same as the rest of us did. So, he, but anyhow, he got by pretty good, but of course, he's passed away a good many years. The whole family, I guess, is going by now. Joe had a pretty hard drinking reputation, too. Oh, yeah, yeah, you bet you are there right now, you. Yeah. Well, I guess that that's what, what got him, I guess, was, oh, it wasn't whiskey he was drinking. No, I can't think of, he shouldn't.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: With moonshine, for one thing, but wasn't it?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No, he got a hold of the wrong bottle. That's what he got a hold of, and he took this here and they said that's what got him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, it wasn't whiskey at all that he drunk?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, I suppose part of it was, too, but he got a hold of this here other bottle, too, and mixed it, and that's what really got him. So, he...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you figure that they were accepted just like any white person.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, right. Yep, just like any other. It was like he used to say, he'd come in and before meal he'd come in and he'd wash, you know, and he says, you know, he says, don't make any difference how much I scrub, it's just as black as ever. Yeah, so... No,… i had good money left out of old Joe already.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The Jansville had a saloon there. Yeah. That's what I heard. Who would drink at it, anyway? Would it be mostly the homesteaders from around there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes. I'll tell you, of course, that's something that has been and always will be. A lot of people, they drink pretty heavy. Yeah, a lot of... it is like living right across from over here, where they say, gosh, what do you do? You can't get out and holler hoopy or anything. No, I says, I always go across the river when I want to be getting holler hoopy. So...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, Elk River was... it had an awful lot of different nationalities working at that mill, didn't it?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, yes. There was... I don't think that there was any Negroes that worked there, but outside of that, well, then, every nationality, I think, that there was, well, then they were there. They were Japs, Chinese, and... yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, how did, how was life in the town like in these earlier years when they had the mill going and everything?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: I'll tell you right now that that was one of the best towns. These fellas, the traveling salesmen and the like of that, they says that Elk River is one of the best towns that we can get in. And... now, we were there in business, that is, and hauling and drying and we'd have to pay the freight and all that stuff, see, end of every month. Well, then we had our bills made up and collected. The first four or five years that we were there, I think all we lost was about ten dollars. That was all we lost. And, gosh, you know, it would run into several hundred dollars a month.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now, you're talking about credit, giving credit?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: That's credit. And... but, gosh, make out the bill, handle it over, payday for them and payday for us. Gosh, here's your money, here's your money. So, it was really good in that way. And everybody had a few dollars. So, people would always pay you back when they... Oh, yes, at the end of the month when payday was... A little extra help every now and then. And there was two of them that had a little spare time. And when they said they were going to come, if they said it was eight o 'clock in the morning or seven o 'clock in the morning, you could be just as sure that they would be there at that time. And it's no... and as far as the money was, whenever you presented the bill, they paid us, there was no questions or anything else. No..., as far as that goes. And the nicest bunch of people. And, oh, some of them would have a little bad luck, some hard luck for them. Yeah, we better chip in a few dollars here in each other's hands and help them out a little bit. And that's what we've done. You know, everybody had a little hard luck. Why, the rest of us were just trying to help them out. Which, you know, was pretty nice.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of hard luck would a good person have?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, a lot of them had sickness. Maybe the house would burn or something, you know. Right after that's what.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have mostly to do with the townspeople or with the lumberjacks?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And the saw millers?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, we had four horses on the... see, they cut up wood at the mill? And then we had four horses on the wagon, that is, to haul wood out from the dump. And, of course, we'd have to look after that. We didn't pay, we just turned in the bill to the company. And they paid us so much a load for hauling, so that took care of that way. But anyway, well then, the only sad part we done, brother, he had a few dollars now and a few extra dollars too. And anybody was leaving there, well then, well, let us sell you the house, let us sell you our house, of course. And we always thought the timber right close there, you know, that that mill would be staying there for years. But instead of that, well, they closed down and they said we'll open in April, but that April was never closed. So, we had one time, we had eight houses there, besides the two that we lived in. And, of course, we, well, there was a couple of them there that we paid two thousand dollars for. But then we sold them for, well, put some furniture in one and we sold it for three hundred and fifty dollars. So, we took a beating on buying the homes there, the houses.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, was there a big difference? I'm trying to figure out what the social life was like in Elk River at the time. And I'm thinking, was mostly the married couples in town, were they, like, did you have much to do with the management people in Elk River? Or was it guys that worked in the saw mill and their wives, or were many of them married?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yeah, you take practically all of them that worked in the mill there, they were married men. Yes, oh, what have, there was always something going on. There was somebody was promoting or something. And, I used to get the biggest kick out of, in the morning, whenever we'd go to work at seven o 'clock in the morning, we'd have to go down and we'd have to haul the freight out of the cars and deliver it to the stores. And, gosh, you know, hey there, did you hear this here story about so-and-so last night? And, no, you'd have to tell this story and, gosh, you know, why you could just laugh till your sights would just hurt, you know. Yeah, I would have your eye on it now, but, no, I kind of wish I was young, follow and then get back in, something like that again, because that was really good.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you think that was a lot more, if you were going to compare life in Elk River to life at Park, how would they stack up one to another?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, of course, you were just kind of by yourself or a little more on the independent side, I imagine, that is when you were at Park. But, still, on the other hand, amusement and like that, and money-wise, well, then Elk River was the place, because we made good money in Elk River.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think people were closer to each other in Park than they were in Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, no, I wouldn't say that that they were, because, of course, there wasn't so many of us at Park, see, so, but they were pretty much still the same. Not much difference among the people. Of course, at Park they were mostly the same nationality, and at Elk River I imagine they were all different kinds of people. Oh, yes, it was, but, I'll tell you, if anybody drifted in there that wasn't a pretty good citizen, well, then he didn't stay very long, because they made it pretty miserable for him now. So, that way, well, then, you know, it just left the, you might say, the best and the good ones there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, who would decide, you know, whether the person was a good person or not? How would they?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, they decided, but as soon as some new fellas drifted in there, it wasn't long until everybody was, well, now, what is here, how is here, and so on. And, by golly, you know, they'd work it down to that he wasn't any good, and by golly, now, if he wasn't, well, then he didn't stay very long.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you know Mr. Bloom at all?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What was he like as the superintendent of the mill there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Bloom, he was, in a way, he was kind of a distant man, but when you got acquainted with him, he was real nice. I liked Bloom. And Charlie Munson, he was, he was another one of the fellas there. Well, I liked him too. Hello. Yeah, yes, and of course, after Bloom passed away, why then, Mrs. Bloom would ever, she'd go anywhere, why, she wouldn't let anybody rope her trunk, because they'd ship it, see, and I'd have to, you know, George E's got to come and tie my trunk up and rope it. And so, they, others then, when she'd called about, she was going away or not, they'd say, okay, now, you go up and rope that trunk, we have no business up there whatsoever, and I'd have to go up and rope her trunk and get things fixed around for her.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did she stay for many years after he died?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, yes, she was there, well, it wasn't too awfully long either, but it was several years that she stayed there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did the Lumberjacks come into Elk River from the camps around a great deal?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, yeah, you take on Saturday nights, you know, when you're riding down there, there was just a lot of them there. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was the Moonshine plentiful around Elk River? I imagine it must have been.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, yes, you betcha. Yeah, there was a lot of it made out there in them woods. And, of course, with our business, why then, I got acquainted with a lot of them, because corn and sugar and all that, and of course, them fellows there that is in Elk River, well, that was, well, the deputy sheriffs and whatnot coming in. But, maybe it's wrong, I don't know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would they be trying to find out from you, you know, who the moonshiners' were?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: That's what they do, you know, they try and find out. And, I'd never, I'd never tell them, I'd just assess that, well, I assess, you know, we're here to make a living, and I assess that they're paying their way, so I have nothing to say. Maybe it was wrong, I don't know, but I didn't feel that taking the moonshiners' money and then go squeal on them, I didn't think that was right either. So...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What can you remember about the kind of places that these moonshiners lived? Did they have just a little cabin up in the woods someplace?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: That's right, they'd either have a cabin or if it wasn't summertime, they'd have a tent. And then they'd get in, that is where they had running water. Yeah, and then, that's the way they lived.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were they lumberjacks, or lumberjack types themselves, do you think?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, some of them were and some of them wasn't. Now, there was a colored man that was there for a while. And that was all he ever done, he never worked or anything, that's all he ever done. And most of them said that he made the best moonshine of any of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever know his name?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Offhand, I couldn't tell you.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's interesting because I haven't heard about him, but then I don't know too much about the Elk River area. I wonder if he'd come from the South because quite a bit of that moonshine, they were Southerners.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: That's right, he did come from the South. You're right, he was from the South. But he had a big trade and anyhow, that's what they all kind of said, that he made the best moonshine of any of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did most of these fellows like this guy, were they able to get by with it and not get caught?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: No. Well, he never got caught and in fact, right around Elk River there, there wasn't too many of them that ever got caught. You know, when I was here, at that time, I was booked, I could vote. And you know, I thought probation would be one of the best things that could be. Because there's so many of these people, if they take a drink, they can't quit. So I thought now, probation is what they need and that'll kind of help take care of this. But I've come to the conclusion, and after being among them bootleggers and that, I've come to the conclusion that I shouldn't have voted that way. It just, as it was, why then, it just throwed everything then as for the bootleggers and that. So I... So it couldn't work, really. It just didn't work. It didn't work. Gosh, you know, why they spent thousands and thousands of dollars, that is, trying to catch up to them and that. But they didn't get anywhere. And there was just as much liquor drank then as there is right today, I imagine.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about in Elk River? Were the sheriffs really rough on any guys that were in town drinking or drunk?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, they... I'd say that they were pretty lenient on them. But still, if they got clear on a place, well then, they'd arrest them and they'd have to pay a fine.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you think it was... I don't know if you would know, but I know like in Potlatch, well that was a company owned town, of course. So there, you know, a person couldn't own any of those houses or anything. Or the business, I guess all the businessmen were salaried. I wonder if that was an attraction of Elk River to a lot of people because there they could make a little money on their own and that sort of thing.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I think you're right. I think that that kind of brought Elk River, of course now, in Elk River, when I first... Well, not when I... Well, when I wanted to move in there and live there with my family, well you know, I couldn't buy a house there either. They were restricted.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: At Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, Elk River, just like Potlatch.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Oh, it was all company owned?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: All company owned there at one time. Yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When was this, that you were trying to buy a house?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I went there in 1925 when I went there. Well then, how come... You said that you later bought a number of houses. Then, they opened it up, see, and they were selling their houses and anybody else that wanted to buy, well you could buy up all the houses you wanted there. Yeah. So, in other words, Elk River was a company owned town, just like Potlatch. Right. At one time it was a company owned town. So...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But the businesses could operate independent of the company.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, they were independent.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, that's kind of funny. They sold their houses just before they shut the town down.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, they just kind of pulled a fast one off us. Yeah, no, that's why I said that if I was big enough, I'd just like to take this plant down here on my shoulders and just dip it upside down. It's kind of a mean way to look at it, but they sure didn't be... No, they wasn't too nice with us fellows that was left there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did it really just change the town completely overnight when they shut down?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh yes, you bet you it changed it. Of course, they were all looking forward to opening up in the spring. It was a bad winter. And they did say that it's so much snow and that we're going to shut down. Because it's just too hard to operate. But, they will open in April. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What winter was this? What year? Do you remember?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, it was in the early 30s was when this year took place. The Depression had already hit then. Yeah. The Depression had hit and it was... Oh, I don't know what this is. But anyhow, it wasn't the early 30s. Because when I went there, I had bought in there with my brother and that. Well then, I said, I'm going to stay here five years. And then I said, I'm going to sell out and move. And gosh, the fifth year when we was there, that was the biggest year that we ever had. And so, he says, why do you think of it now? Well, I said, I think I better stay. You know, I said, because G .I. says our business. I said, yes. And the money we're making now, I said, we can hardly afford to quit. And it was, well, about six, I think this was about the sixth year then. Then this one less hit. And of course, everything went to pieces. When the mill didn't run, there wasn't anything there. There wasn't any camps close by either that was operating. So there wasn't anything there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did most of the people move out of town right away or did this gradually move away?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, they gradually moved away. I think maybe it occurs to me, of course never being there, but just from what I would imagine, that it would have been really rough on kind of separating people that had grown to be friends and knew each other and liked the town. Right, it was. You know, we really didn't like to. We liked to do part, but then it was one of them things. Yeah. Now, Mrs. Clark's dad, see, he had the butcher shop up there. And of course at that time, well, it was the same all over. A butcher shop was a butcher shop. Maybe they had a keg of pickles or a keg of sauerkraut or something like that that they'd have, that is to sell to go with their mates. But now, a butcher shop, well then you could go right down here into a drug store and you could go down there and you could buy that low cost. You could go in there and buy anything practically that you want. And that has made it rough. That has made it rough. I think that like at that time, well then, a butcher shop was a butcher shop and a store, well then they'd sell clothing and like that. And a drug store, it was kind of by itself, but of today, well then you go into any of these places and you can buy anything that you, practically anything you want.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Is there any, what happened in the business community, like what happened to your business at that time? Did it just go down the drain? Yeah, it just went right down there, right?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: You betcha… and then my brother and I, that was in the Depression, the company sold a lot of their stuff. Even their old shovels, steam shovels that they had. So my brother and I, we got in the head that we was gonna go plaster mining. And so then, old T .P. Jones and they had a lease on some land. And so then, by golly, we got a shovel and so we went mining. And well, I didn't mine, but my brother did. He was the main miner. And then there was a couple of fellas that we knew that, well, they were shovel runners and like that, so we got them and we mined there for about three years. And we didn't do too bad. Of course, there was too many of us in on it. That was the trouble. There was too many of us in on it. So, then we finally decided to quit mining. No, when the town folded up, I went to work for the Clearwater Highway District. I went to work for the Clearwater Highway District. And I, well, I stayed with them for about fourteen years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you stay at Elk River?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, I still lived in Elk River.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What kind of a difference did it make in social life before and after?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, gosh. You know, you'd come into town in the evening and it was just so quiet there that nothing's stirring at all. No, sir, nothing's stirring at all. So, it was, but anyhow, then when I, well, I went to work, that is, and then the equipment, the highway district, they loaned out their equipment, that is, to the state. See, they had, the state had to take care of the road from Elk River to Bovill. And so then, I was kind of their main man. So, then I, so I was between the state and the highway district. That's where I was working. I had the equipment.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You ran the equipment yourself?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, I ran the equipment myself. So, that way, well then, then I, well, the state, they wouldn't furnish me anything. That is, not like gravel or like that. And gosh, I just fought that mud all the time. And so then, anyhow, well then, one day, well then, I wasn't feeling too good. And the fellow I told, he was from the state, and he came up. And we was out, we was out on the road, and he says, gosh, your road is in bad shape. And I says, and you fellas don't give me anything to fix it with either. I says, we're gonna fill a hole. I says, we've got to get up here and dig it out. And I said, pick and shovel and shovel it on, and we don't get nowhere with it. And so then, oh well, he says, it's gonna get better some of these days. Well, I says, as far as with me, I says, you can just take me off from your list. I says, I'm quitting. Well, what are we gonna do with equipment?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: I says, it's going back to the color where I am in East. I says that I just kind of ate up my mind that I've been here long enough. And so then, oh, he says, you're not gonna quit, so you're still gonna stay with us. No, I says that I have fought this and fought it. So I says that I'm through. And so then, there was, oh, for a little Birchmier, he was the highway super, or the street super, down at that Moscow. And in early days in farming, with that hauling grain to Deary, well, we've been up there. He lived on Texas Ridge at that time. So, he used to come up there and fish, and so then, he was in there getting his supper that evening, and he says to the woman in there, he says, how's this been? He says, he's been in a lot of Torgerson behavior himself. And she says, we're gonna lose him. He says, he's held in his resignation, and he's equipped, and he's moving away. And, has there an idea where he's moving?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, he did say that his children was getting ready for the university, or getting out of the high school, so that's kind of where he plans to go. But he, I'm not sure that he's going to Moscow, but then somewhere he's got to go to. And so then, he says, I wonder where he's at? And, well, she says that they're having doings at the schoolhouse this evening, and she says, I'm pretty sure there's where he is. But he says, they generally take in all them doings like that, and I got you know, here you come. And so, they, he told them who he wanted, and they says that, well, we'll get them for you. So then they come in, and Georgia's your wallet. And so I went out, and there he was. He says to me, he says that, they tell me that you're gonna leave. Yeah. I says, I have turned in everything, so I says, I'm all free now to go. And he says, are you coming to Moscow?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, I says, I kind of think that's where we better move to. And my first wife, she had some kin folks there in Moscow, and so on and so on. Anyhow, then, we thought that would be a pretty good place to go. And so then he says, you'll come and work for me, won't you? And, well, I says, I better not make any promises. I says, you know, there's times when I've thought that I'd kind of like to be a carpenter. I says, I'd like to just kind of hammer up and make some black nails. And I says, cuss a little bit and that. But, well, he says, you know, he says, I need a man. And he says, I'd like to have you come. And, well, I says, I don't like to promise you. And I says, if I promise you, that's what I'm gonna do. Well, he says, make one promise, and that is you're gonna come and you'll go to work with me. Okay, I says, but now I don't want you to feel bad if I don't stay. Well, then, I don't want you to feel bad if I quit. For I says, you know, I've always thought that that was the only privilege, really, that a working man had. If he didn't like it, he could quit. No, no, he says, that's fine. He says, if you don't like it, well, he says, that's just all right. Went there and dug, you know, stayed there 20 years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What did you do for him?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, I went to work and say, oh, whatever equipment that was to do, and I was kind of his right-hand man. And then, about five years, he passed away, and then I took over the street superintendent job. In Moscow. I didn't like to, there wasn't any of us that liked to leave, but still, we were near had to. And, of course, my children, we were already paying for two of them, that is, in Moscow going to the university. And so then, we had two more coming up with, three boys and a girl, and that's what the family was. So, we went there. I didn't think that I was, well, I wasn't sure, I didn't know. Of course, I had quite a lot of experience, you know, in heavy equipment, and so on, so. You've mentioned before that the Dre business was doing extremely well, right up until the town went down. Oh, yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Why do you think the business was good? What was most of the work that you folks were doing there?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, there in town, well then we had two teams there, working, that is, for the hall and freight and delivery. We had two deliveries to make. One in the morning at nine, and the other one at four o 'clock in the afternoon. And then, we had a truck, and then I moved quite a lot of people away from there. I done a lot of moving. So, between all of it, well then that, he was pretty nice.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: These deliveries, you say, in the morning and afternoon, they were just all over town?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: They were all over town.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: From the merchants?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: From the merchants. There was three stores there, and we delivered from all three of them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Three stores before the mill went out?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, there was three stores there at that time. And, no, they done a good business, I'll tell you right now. Yeah, there was, and, you know, there was, a lot of times we had a hundred boxes to go out. And, I don't know if you ever seen, but they're the collapsible ones that were just, when you put your groceries in it, while you opened it up, and then when it come to, you were through, all you had to do was just collapse it, and it just all lay right down flat. No, I haven't seen them. Yeah, yes, that's what we had up there. No, we kept busy, and then we hauled wood. Some of them fellas go out and cut some wood up in the woods, and we'd have to haul wood and...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Or into town?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Or into town for others, yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you take care of the horses?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yeah. You know, we had, well, we had a room in our barn, that is for Six Head. And, then the company, then, we hired a stall down there, and we had two horses down there also. Of course, then when we began to haul the wood, well, then we had all four horses down there in the company barn. So...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, do you think that there was a lot of resentment in the town when the mill was taken out? Do you think that for a time people were very angry?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Oh, yes, you bet you're right. Now, there was just lots of them that... Well, they wasn't ready to move, and some of them had spent their money, you might say, for something, or this or that, and it just left them in real hard circumstances. Did, was there any...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did people try, was there any effort that they could make to try to get the company to change their mind, or try to buy the mill, or something like that? Was there anything you could do?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: I'll tell you, there wasn't a thing you could do. They just, when they got ready to clean up in there and that, they just got boxcars and loaded that mill, they, well, they did bring some of it down here at Lewiston, but now, like the older stuff and that that they couldn't use, why, they just loaded it in a car and shipped it out, and it went to Japan. That's where it went. No, I tell you, that was one thing about them, they didn't ask any odds or ends or anything about anybody. It's, they done it, and that was it. No, I tell you, I know, that potlatch, you know, they, they, well, though I've got my oldest boy and his wife, she's worked with the potlatch now for 32 years. She started in in the mobile office, so, and my boy then, he's, well, he's got 20, about 20 years, I guess, in the middle of the two. But it sounds like, they really didn't, it sounds like they really could be pretty hard on people. I mean, they could do things without any care about them. And they, they didn't show that they cared about the people. But now, what I'm gonna say about my son and daughter-in-law, they were at Bovill, and so then when they closed up Bovill there, well then they moved them into, or that is, they, well, they were gonna leave one or two men there, that would be the limit up there. And so then they wanted to move up to headquarters up there, and so then they said, no, we're not going up to headquarters. There's plenty of snow, and bad enough right here, and we're far enough in here, we can get out, if we want to go into Spokane, we want to go anywhere, we can get out from here. So if you haven't got anything else, only headquarters, why, you might as well take our name off your list. And so then, oh no, they said that we don't want to do that, but we need you in headquarters. Well, we're not moving. So, and so then, in a little day or so, by then they come around and they said, would you move to St. Mary's?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: And they said, yes, we'll move to St. Mary's. And how soon can you move? Well, just put in there any time, well we're gonna have a truck here to move you. Is it a week? Would that be alright? And so then they said, well, I know we can sell our home here, so a week will be alright, and even if the house sets empty for a few days, well that's okay. But anyhow, in a week's time, well then they moved to St. Mary's, and they've been there now I think about six years, they've been to St. Mary's. So, I suppose I should feel too hurt about the PFI, because they give them a living and put a good wage in it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What does she do for them?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: She works in the office up there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And what does he do?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: And he works there also. He's an accountant, he's an accountant. I was thinking about some of these different groups that were in the mill in Elk River in those days, and I have heard that there were a couple of Japanese businessmen in Elk River.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were they there when you were there? There was a photographer and a dentist, were they there when you were there? Do you remember anything about those two fellas? Unusual to have Japanese businessmen in a small town.

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: As far as that goes, they didn't stay too long. They wasn't there very long. So, but now the laundry, now that was Chinese laundry. And then there was a chap that worked down there in the mill, and he was lumber grader. He graded lumber, this chap did. And a pool player. By God, I'll tell you right now that he was a pool player. Yeah, he'd sure clean up on them fellas, you know what I mean? But them others, they didn't stay long.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you get to know that grader, this fella?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Yeah, I knew him. I used to get down in the evening sometimes rather. I'd get around the pool house. And I used to shoot a little pool too. But, golly wish, I couldn't begin to play with him. But anyhow, I'd try, I'd just get out there and just show them that I was kind of a sport anyhow. But, no.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: These other guys, wouldn't they know he was a good player too? Why would they even try to beat him?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: Well, there was other fellas there that were good pool players too. But, I'll tell you right now, he was just about the best that I have ever seen.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could he run a whole, a straight rack?

segments.speaker: George Torgerson
segments.words: A lot of times he'd do it. Yeah, a lot of times he'd do it. Of course, I think that there was times that he would just let the other fella, you know, let them win. Because they had to win once in a while. But, I think that that was just why he'd done it. He'd just make a bad play or something like that. And, no, he was, he was sure.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
